Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 302 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
WMU 302 is located west of Pincher Creek, Alberta 
and South of Lundbreck, Alberta. It is bordered by 
highways 6 and 3, Drywood creek in the south and the 
provincial forest reserve and castle provincial park on 
the west. It consists of foothills, grasslands and 
cropland habitats. WMU 302 has good quality habitat 
for moose, elk, and both deer species. WMU 302 was 
also surveyed specifically for elk in 2015. 
Survey Method 
A rotary wing (A-star B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 11,2025 flying 20 east-west lines 
at 1.85 km intervals, with 48 per cent coverage (800 m 
wide survey strip, area surveyed 354 km2) for a total 
linear survey effort of 442 km. At each observation 
point, ungulates were classified by species, and when 
possible, sex and age were recorded.  
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose 
was calculated by multiplying the number of animals 
per transect (Σx) by total area (km2) searched (total 
survey strip area [Σz]) (Jolly 1969, as described in 
Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area (km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with a 90 per cent confidence intervals. 
Confidence interval width was calculated by 
multiplying the t statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the 
Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error 
(SE; without replacement) of the abundance estimate 
where SE=sq root variance, and variance = N*(N-n)/ 
(n*(n-1))*(Σx2+R2*ΣZ2-2*R*Σxz) with N as the total 
number of possible transects given 100 per cent 
coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  
Moose, deer and elk observations made during the 
survey were recorded even if outside of the transect 
width. Moose, mule deer and white-tailed deer data 
points were truncated to 800m strip width for 
population estimates. All elk observations were 
summed for a minimum total count.   
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 324 mule deer were observed on transect 
with an average group size of 6.6 (range 1-21). The 
estimated density was 0.91 mule deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 649 individuals (90 per cent 
CI 451 – 847). A total of 286 mule deer were 
successfully classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio 
was estimated to be 34:100:59. Due to the timing of 
the survey being mid-February, a small amount of 
antler drop had occurred which will affect these ratios.  
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 602 white-tailed deer were observed on 
transect with an average group size of 6.4 (range 1-
36). The estimated density was 1.7 deer/km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 1205 individuals (90 per 
cent CI 841-1570). White-tailed deer were not 
classified into sex and age cohorts due to extensive 
antler drop having occurred by the time the survey was 
conducted. The 2025 population estimate represents 
the only statistically rigorous method employed for 
white-tailed deer in WMU 302.  
Moose 
A total of 61 moose were observed on transect with 
and average group size of 1.5 (range 1-3). The 
estimated density was 0.17 moose/ km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 122 individuals (90 per cent 
CI 94 - 150). Moose were generally counted 
anecdotally in past surveys for a minimum total count, 
which likely greatly underestimated the population. 
Elk 
A total of 668 elk were observed with an average 
group size of 59 (range 1-242). The bull:cow:calf ratio 
was found to be 11:100:26. The past surveys are 
presented in Table 1. The elk population in 2025 is 
41% lower than that reported in 2015.
